newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks plunge in freefall sparked by banks.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks plunge in freefall sparked by banks.

text.p: Japanese shares plunged more than three percent to their lowest level in more than a year on Thursday in a continuing freefall sparked by worries that the nation's major banks cannot solve their huge debt problems.
Analysts said they are concerned that the sell-off is a vicious cycle, since the fall reduces the value of investments held by the big banks and therefore prompts investors to keep selling.

The Nikkei 225 share index, the market's main barometer, fell 606.51 points to end at 18,073.87, a fall of 3.25 percent. Since trading opened for the year on Monday, the index has fallen nearly 1,300 points.
Japan's major banks are still trying to cope with problem loans left over from the economic boom and bust of the 1980s.
"The weakness of the banking issues is depressing sectors such as real estate and construction, darkening sentiment as a whole," a trader at a foreign securities house said.
Government officials have been trying to downplay the situation. A senior official at the Ministry of Finance told Reuters on Thursday that the economy is not as bad as the market seems to think.
Others were less upbeat.
The chairman of Japan's Chamber of Commerce said a continued fall in shares could cause "grave problems" as Japanese companies close their books at the end of the fiscal year on March 31.
Some brokers said that the sell-off was also being sparked by the upcoming "Big Bang" financial reforms being pushed hard by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
The reforms will make it less attractive for big Japanese companies to hold shares in each other, prompting sales in the bank shares.
"Foreign brokerages' sales of bank shares and dissolving of cross-shareholdings hit the market hard," one broker said.

Another concern is that Japanese investors will cover their losses at home by selling investments overseas, which could put pressure on other markets. Japan is among the world's biggest holders of U.S. Treasury securities.
The sell-off has also been prompted in part by the fall in the Japanese yen against the dollar. In late trading, the dollar was quoted at 116.30 yen, up from 115.80 yen in New York.
Faced with the weaknesses elsewhere, government bonds were slightly higher, although they closed below their peaks of the day.
Where some saw worries, others saw buying opportunities.
"Despite the sharp decline, the sell-off was more technical than panic-driven," said Haruo Nakaharu, director at Toyo Securities Co Ltd.
"Market participants feel stocks should fall as far as they want so that the only direction left is up."
The question analysts have not yet answered, however, is how far that is.
They noted that when stocks plunged to the 14,000 level in 1992, the government stepped in and bought shares in what was called a "price-keeping operation".
But there appears to be little chance of that currently, traders said, especially with a government committed to less interference in the economy.

Other stock indices fared just as badly, with TOPIX down 41.10 points or 2.87 percent at 1,392.18. The Nikkei 300 lost 8.09 points or 2.96 percent to 264,90. The second-section index slid 30.89 points or 1.71 percent to 1,771.54. Turnover was 9.69 million shares against 7.58 million on Wednesday.
